paper.title: CaBP1 and 2 enable sustained CaV1.3 calcium currents and synaptic transmission in inner hair cells
paper.abstract: To encode continuous sound stimuli, the inner hair cell (IHC) ribbon synapses utilize calcium-binding proteins (CaBPs), which reduce the inactivation of their CaV1.3 calcium channels. Mutations in the CABP2 gene underlie non-syndromic autosomal recessive hearing loss DFNB93. Besides CaBP2, the structurally related CaBP1 is highly abundant in the IHCs. Here, we investigated how the two CaBPs cooperatively regulate IHC synaptic function. In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, we find strongly enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation, slowed recovery from inactivation and impaired sustained exocytosis. Already mild IHC activation further reduces the availability of channels to trigger synaptic transmission and may effectively silence synapses. Spontaneous and sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced and strongly depend on stimulation rates. Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity. We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.

nodes.label: CaBP1 and CaBP2 together provide sufficient attenuation of CaV1.3 channel inacti…
nodes.claim: CaBP1 and CaBP2 together provide sufficient attenuation of CaV1.3 channel inactivation at IHC ribbon synapses to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission, and their combined loss causes severe hearing impairment that is partially rescuable by CaBP2 gene therapy.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Together, they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at this synapse.

strengths: The paper provides multi-level evidence spanning from single-channel biophysics (VDI/CDI quantification) through synaptic function (exocytosis) to systems-level hearing (ABRs, SGN recordings), creating a coherent narrative.

The DKO phenotype is dramatically more severe than either single KO, consistent with the claimed synergistic/overlapping role, and aligns with prior work showing CaBPs suppress CaV1.3 inactivation (Haeseleer et al., 2000; Picher, 2017).
The gene therapy rescue experiment provides a causal test linking CaBP2 expression to restoration of channel function, exocytosis, and hearing.
weaknesses: The claim of 'indefatigable neurotransmission' is strong language not fully supported: even WT IHCs show some inactivation, and the paper does not demonstrate truly indefatigable transmission.

The rescue is explicitly partial — thresholds do not fully recover, and the paper acknowledges possible irreversible changes and confounding effects of missing CaBP1. The claim that gene therapy is viable is overstated for a proof-of-concept with incomplete recovery.

The comparison across genotypes (DKO vs single KOs) relies partly on previously published data acquired under potentially different conditions (different tonotopic positions for Cabp2-KO, different ages, different labs), weakening the quantitative comparison.
The claim of 'temporally precise' neurotransmission is not directly tested in WT with CaBP manipulation; rather it is inferred from the loss-of-function phenotype.
alternative_interpretations: The hearing impairment could partly reflect developmental consequences of chronic Ca2+ signaling disruption (e.g., reduced BK channel expression, altered synaptic morphology) rather than solely acute channel inactivation.
Off-target effects of CaBP2 overexpression (acknowledged by the authors, citing Oestreicher et al., 2021) could contribute to the rescue phenotype through mechanisms unrelated to CaV1.3 modulation.
required_assumptions: CaBP1 and CaBP2 are the dominant modulators of CaV1.3 inactivation in IHCs, with negligible contribution from CaBP4, CaBP5, or other mechanisms.
The DKO phenotype primarily reflects loss of CaBP function in IHCs rather than other cell types.
In vitro electrophysiology at room temperature with perforated patch faithfully reflects in vivo channel behavior.
evaluation.notes: This is a composite root claim aggregating several sub-claims, some of which are better supported than others. The gene therapy claim is the weakest link due to incomplete rescue and lack of controls for surgical effects.

nodes.label: Combined loss of CaBP1 and CaBP2 dramatically enhances both VDI and CDI of IHC C…
nodes.claim: Combined loss of CaBP1 and CaBP2 dramatically enhances both VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, far beyond what is observed in either single knockout.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs

strengths: Direct quantification of VDI and CDI using Ba2+/Ca2+ substitution following the established Tadross et al. (2010) method provides rigorous separation of inactivation types.
Both VDI (~2-fold increase) and CDI (~6-fold increase) are dramatically enhanced in DKO, with highly significant p-values (p<0.0001).
The comparison with single KOs (Picher, 2017; Yang et al., 2018) demonstrates synergistic enhancement beyond either single KO, strengthening the claim of combined effects.
The observation that CaBP2 loss alone primarily affects VDI (Picher, 2017) while the DKO massively enhances CDI is a novel finding suggesting CaBP1 contributes substantially to CDI suppression.
weaknesses: The comparison with single KO data relies on previously published recordings that may have been acquired under slightly different conditions (e.g., the Cabp2-KO data was from lower apex/mid-cochlear positions).
Sample sizes for VDI/CDI analysis are not explicitly stated in the text for the 2 mM divalent condition.
The claim 'far beyond what is observed in either single knockout' depends partly on historical data; ideally all genotypes would be recorded simultaneously with identical protocols.
alternative_interpretations: Enhanced inactivation could partly reflect compensatory downregulation of other modulatory proteins (e.g., changes in CaV1.3 splice variants or auxiliary subunits) rather than solely the direct absence of CaBP-mediated modulation.
required_assumptions: Ba2+ currents faithfully report VDI without confounding effects of Ba2+ on channel gating beyond blocking CDI.
The Tadross et al. (2010) formalism accurately separates VDI and CDI in IHC CaV1.3 channels.
Comparison across studies with different conditions and tonotopic positions is valid.
evaluation.notes: This is one of the best-supported claims in the paper with direct electrophysiological measurements and appropriate controls.

nodes.label: The combined absence of CaBP1 and CaBP2 almost abolishes sustained exocytosis an…
nodes.claim: The combined absence of CaBP1 and CaBP2 almost abolishes sustained exocytosis and impairs exocytosis efficiency beyond what can be explained by reduced Ca2+ influx, suggesting additional roles for CaBPs in synaptic processes.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.

strengths: Capacitance measurements directly quantify exocytosis, and the impairment of sustained exocytosis is statistically significant at multiple time points.
The reduced exocytosis efficiency (ΔCm/QCa) points to an additional mechanism beyond reduced Ca2+ influx, which is an important observation.
Rescue by CaBP2 expression reverses the efficiency deficit, supporting a causal link to CaBP function.
The finding that neither single KO shows this exocytosis defect (Picher, 2017; Yang et al., 2018) establishes the novel synergistic phenotype.
weaknesses: The claim that CaBPs have 'additional roles in synaptic processes' beyond channel modulation is speculative and not directly tested. The reduced efficiency could reflect indirect consequences of altered Ca2+ dynamics (e.g., different Ca2+ microdomain geometry due to faster channel inactivation).

The exocytosis efficiency calculation assumes a simple linear relationship between QCa and ΔCm, but the relationship between Ca2+ and exocytosis is highly nonlinear and depends on the spatiotemporal profile of Ca2+ signals, which would be fundamentally altered by enhanced inactivation.
Endocytic contributions to ΔCm measurements during long stimuli could confound the interpretation of sustained exocytosis.
The authors note but do not adequately address that cells used for train stimuli had lower-than-average inactivation (0.36 vs 0.47), introducing selection bias.
alternative_interpretations: The apparent reduction in exocytosis efficiency could be entirely explained by the altered spatiotemporal profile of Ca2+ at active zones due to rapid inactivation, rather than a direct CaBP role in vesicle fusion/replenishment.

If CaV1.3 channels inactivate rapidly during sustained stimulation, the remaining Ca2+ influx may be carried by channels at non-synaptic locations, inflating QCa relative to synaptically relevant Ca2+, thus artifactually reducing the efficiency ratio.
CaBP1 and 2 modulation of CaMKII (Haeseleer et al., 2000) could affect otoferlin phosphorylation (Meese et al., 2017), but this is entirely speculative without direct evidence.
required_assumptions: ΔCm/QCa is a valid proxy for exocytosis efficiency, and QCa proportionally reflects Ca2+ available at release sites.
Endocytic contributions during long stimuli are comparable between genotypes.
The nonlinear Ca2+-exocytosis relationship does not confound the efficiency calculation.
evaluation.notes: The claim of 'additional roles beyond channel modulation' is the weakest part. The reduced efficiency could be a secondary consequence of altered Ca2+ dynamics rather than a direct CaBP role in exocytosis.

nodes.label: Cabp1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe, progressive hearing impairment with drastica…
nodes.claim: Cabp1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe, progressive hearing impairment with drastically impaired sound encoding by spiral ganglion neurons.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Already in young (3- to 4-week-old) Cabp1/2-DKO animals, ABR thresholds were highly elevated, with tone bursts up to a maximum intensity of 90 dB SPL barely eliciting any ABR response.

strengths: ABR thresholds are unambiguously elevated at 3-4 weeks with clear progression by 7-13 weeks, documented with adequate sample sizes (N=7-9).
Multi-method assessment (ABR thresholds, wave amplitudes, latencies, SGN single-unit recordings) provides convergent evidence.
The SGN recording data, despite low yield (0.3 vs 2.5 neurons/hour), shows dramatically impaired sound encoding with quantitative statistics.
Progressive nature documented across two age groups.
Consistent with the known DFNB93 phenotype in humans (Schrauwen et al., 2012; Picher, 2017).
weaknesses: SGN recordings suffer from severe selection bias: only neurons with residual activity could be detected, potentially missing the most severely affected neurons entirely.
The classification of some DKO units as SGNs vs cochlear nucleus neurons is acknowledged as uncertain (13 of 16 assumed SGNs, 3 potentially bushy/multipolar cells).
The authors cannot exclude contributions from impaired mechanotransduction, as noted in the discussion.
DPOAEs were reduced in about half of DKO animals, complicating the claim that the deficit is purely IHC synaptic.
alternative_interpretations: Some hearing impairment could reflect outer hair cell dysfunction given the DPOAE abnormalities in ~50% of animals.
Progressive impairment could reflect neurodegeneration secondary to reduced synaptic activity rather than worsening channel function per se.
required_assumptions: The hearing impairment is primarily synaptic rather than reflecting mechanotransduction or cochlear amplification deficits.
The SGN recording yield difference reflects genuine physiological differences rather than technical factors.
evaluation.notes: The hearing impairment itself is very well documented. The 'progressive' component and attribution to specific mechanisms have some caveats.

nodes.label: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse, wi…
nodes.claim: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse, with each partially compensating for the loss of the other.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Our findings indicate that the functions of CaBP1 and 2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse.

strengths: The logic is compelling: if DKO >> single KO phenotypes, the remaining CaBP must partially compensate in each single KO.
This is supported at multiple levels: channel inactivation, exocytosis, hearing thresholds, and SGN spiking.
Consistent with the high structural homology between CaBP1 and CaBP2 (Haeseleer et al., 2000).

The observation that CaBP1 loss alone has minimal early effects (Yang et al., 2018) while CaBP2 loss causes progressive impairment (Picher, 2017), yet their combined loss is devastating, logically supports partial overlap with CaBP2 being the more critical player.
weaknesses: The paper does not directly demonstrate that CaBP1 compensates in Cabp2-KO IHCs (e.g., by showing upregulation of CaBP1 in Cabp2-KO or by rescue experiments with CaBP1 overexpression).

The conclusion of 'partial overlap' could alternatively reflect non-overlapping additive effects (i.e., each protein independently prevents a fraction of inactivation, and their combined loss is simply additive rather than reflecting functional redundancy).
No protein-level quantification of CaBP1 in Cabp2-KO IHCs (or vice versa) is provided to test compensatory upregulation.
alternative_interpretations: Rather than functional overlap (each can do the other's job), the two proteins might independently suppress different aspects or pools of inactivation, and the DKO phenotype is simply additive.
The synergistic phenotype could partly reflect loss of CaBP heterodimerization or cooperative binding effects rather than simple redundancy.
required_assumptions: The DKO phenotype reflects direct loss of CaBP function rather than developmental or compensatory changes unique to the DKO.
CaBP1 and CaBP2 modulate the same pool of CaV1.3 channels.
evaluation.notes: The claim of partial overlap is well-supported by the comparative phenotypic data, though the mechanistic basis (redundancy vs. additivity) is not resolved.

nodes.label: Viral delivery of CaBP2 substantially rescues auditory function in DKO animals, …
nodes.claim: Viral delivery of CaBP2 substantially rescues auditory function in DKO animals, supporting the view that reversible CaV1.3 inactivation is the main mechanism of hearing loss in CaBP-related deafness and that gene therapy is a viable treatment strategy.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This successful viral rescue supports the view that a reversible inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 currents is the main mechanism of hearing loss in CaBP-related deafness, which can be targeted by gene therapy in the future.

strengths: The rescue experiment is well-designed: viral delivery of CaBP2 produces measurable improvements in CaV1.3 inactivation, exocytosis, and ABR thresholds/amplitudes.
The approach follows prior successful work (Oestreicher et al., 2021) with the same vector system.
Suprathreshold ABR responses were restored to WT-like levels, demonstrating substantial functional recovery.
The partial rescue supports the interpretation that the phenotype is primarily due to reversible channel inactivation rather than irreversible developmental defects.
weaknesses: The rescue is explicitly incomplete: ABR thresholds did not fully recover, and Ca2+ current inactivation was only partially restored. This undermines the strong claim that 'reversible CaV1.3 inactivation is the main mechanism.'
The gene therapy uses only the L-isoform of CaBP2, while the alt-isoform may be more abundant in IHCs (Yang et al., 2016). This is a significant design limitation.
No controls for surgical effects on hearing are mentioned for the injected ears.

CaBP1 remains absent in rescued animals, so the rescue cannot be attributed solely to CaBP2 restoring normal CaV1.3 function — it may also partly reflect CaBP2 overexpression compensating in ways distinct from its normal function.
The claim that gene therapy is 'viable' is premature: this is a proof-of-concept in mice with an incomplete rescue, no long-term follow-up data, and no demonstration of safety.
Possible adverse effects of exogenous CaBP2 overexpression are acknowledged but not systematically assessed.
alternative_interpretations: The incomplete rescue could indicate that irreversible developmental changes (e.g., reduced BK expression, altered synaptic morphology) contribute significantly to the phenotype and cannot be reversed by later CaBP2 expression.
The suprathreshold over-recovery (wave I amplitudes larger than expected) might reflect pathological overexpression effects rather than normal restoration.
Recovery might be partly due to non-specific effects of AAV transduction or surgical procedure.
required_assumptions: The L-isoform of CaBP2 is functionally equivalent to the native alt-isoform in IHCs.
The timing of gene delivery (postnatal) is sufficient to reverse effects that may have accumulated during development.
Partial rescue demonstrates the principle despite incomplete recovery.
Surgical procedure does not independently affect hearing outcomes.
evaluation.notes: The claim about gene therapy viability is the most speculative part of the paper. The rescue data is encouraging but the interpretation overreaches the evidence.

nodes.label: The severity of the synaptic phenotype is strongly activity-dependent: even mild…
nodes.claim: The severity of the synaptic phenotype is strongly activity-dependent: even mild stimulation drives CaV1.3 channels into prolonged inactivation in the absence of CaBPs, and in vivo a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels are predicted to be in a state of prolonged inactivation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We propose that in vivo in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels are in a state of prolonged inactivation.

strengths: Multiple experimental approaches demonstrate activity-dependence: holding potential variation (-85 to -55 mV), sine wave amplitude variation, and in vivo stimulus rate variation all converge on the same conclusion.
The in vivo SGN data showing rate-dependent recovery (0.2-0.5 Hz plateau in DKO vs 150 ms in WT) provides compelling physiological validation.
The 2-min sine wave experiments revealing slow recovery with a double-exponential component in DKO IHCs are novel and informative.
Consistent with the concept of deep-state inactivation described for other voltage-gated channels (Bezanilla et al., 1982; Payandeh et al., 2012).
weaknesses: The prediction that 'in vivo a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels are in a state of prolonged inactivation' is an extrapolation from in vitro data at room temperature. In vivo conditions (body temperature, endogenous Ca2+ buffering, resting potential) may differ substantially.
The sine wave stimulation protocol is an approximation of in vivo conditions; actual receptor potentials are more complex.

The paradoxical finding that recovery after 500-ms depolarization is fastest in DKO (where the most inactivation occurs) complicates the interpretation and is explained post hoc with a Ca2+ clearance hypothesis that is not directly tested.
alternative_interpretations: The activity-dependent worsening could partly reflect rundown of Ca2+ currents or dialysis effects during prolonged recordings rather than solely deep-state inactivation.
The in vivo stimulus rate effects could partly reflect synaptic vesicle depletion rather than solely CaV1.3 recovery kinetics.
required_assumptions: In vitro holding potential manipulations and sine wave stimulation adequately model in vivo IHC activity.
Room temperature recordings faithfully predict in vivo behavior at body temperature.
The deep-state inactivation model from other channels applies to CaV1.3 in IHCs.
evaluation.notes: This is one of the most interesting and well-supported claims, though the extrapolation to in vivo conditions requires caution.

nodes.label: The hearing impairment in DKO animals is primarily due to defects in IHC functio…
nodes.claim: The hearing impairment in DKO animals is primarily due to defects in IHC function rather than SGN dysfunction or impaired cochlear amplification.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Since Cabp1 KO animals show normal hearing several weeks after birth, and CaBP2 is absent from SGNs, we interpret the hearing impairment of the Cabp1/2 DKO animals to be primarily due to defects of hair cell function and judge contribution by SGN dysfunction as rather unlikely

strengths: The argument is logical: CaBP2 is absent from SGNs (Yang et al., 2016), and CaBP1 KO alone has normal early hearing (Yang et al., 2018), so SGN dysfunction from CaBP1 loss alone should be minimal.
The DPOAE data suggests largely preserved cochlear amplification in most DKO animals.
The IHC-level electrophysiology (channel inactivation, exocytosis impairment) provides a clear mechanism for the hearing deficit.
weaknesses: DPOAEs are reduced in ~50% of DKO animals, which the authors acknowledge but downplay. This suggests outer hair cell dysfunction may contribute in a significant fraction of animals.

The paper does not directly test or rule out SGN dysfunction. CaBP1 (caldendrin isoform) is expressed in SGNs (Yang et al., 2016), and its loss could affect SGN excitability or survival, particularly in combination with reduced synaptic drive.
The BK channel reduction could affect IHC receptor potentials and thus contribute to hearing impairment through a mechanism distinct from synaptic CaV1.3 inactivation.
The authors cannot exclude mechanotransduction defects, as they explicitly acknowledge, and note similarities between CaBPs and CIB2 (associated with hair bundle defects).
No direct recordings of IHC receptor potentials are provided.
alternative_interpretations: SGN dysfunction due to loss of caldendrin (CaBP1 splice variant) could contribute to hearing impairment, especially at later ages.
Outer hair cell dysfunction (evidenced by reduced DPOAEs in half the animals) could contribute significantly to elevated thresholds.
Reduced BK channel expression could impair IHC receptor potential dynamics, contributing to hearing loss independently of CaV1.3 inactivation.
CaBP interactions with CIB2 or mechanotransduction components (Giese et al., 2017; Riazuddin et al., 2012) could affect hair bundle function.
required_assumptions: CaBP1 loss in SGNs does not significantly affect SGN function.
Outer hair cell dysfunction in ~50% of animals is either minor or unrelated to CaBP loss.
BK channel reduction does not significantly contribute to the hearing phenotype.
Mechanotransduction is normal in DKO IHCs.
evaluation.notes: This claim requires multiple assumptions that are not directly tested. The DPOAE findings in particular weaken the claim that cochlear amplification is fully preserved.

In heterologous systems (Haeseleer et al., 2004), CaBP effects may differ due to absence of native IHC protein partners.
required_assumptions: The shift is a genuine biophysical effect rather than an artifact of the recording conditions.
evaluation.notes: The surprise finding is transparently reported but unexplained, which is appropriate.
